questions.q: Per this lesson, what happens to a glossary that anyone can edit freely, with no approval process?
options: It degrades fast — definitions drift as people edit back and forth with no record of who changed what
It automatically becomes more accurate over time
It requires no maintenance at all
It is legally required to be open-edit in every organization
questions.explain: Without governance, a glossary inherits a wiki page's reliability problems — careful definitions drift back into vagueness with no accountability trail.

questions.q: Which of these correctly lists the four term lifecycle states in order, per this lesson?
options: Draft, in review, approved, deprecated
Approved, draft, deprecated, in review
In review, deprecated, draft, approved
Deprecated, approved, draft, in review
questions.explain: A term moves from a flagged, unofficial draft, through review with rationale, to the official approved state, and eventually to deprecated once retired.

questions.q: According to this lesson, who should typically hold approval authority for a glossary term?
options: The business steward accountable for that domain
The IT department, since they maintain the glossary tool
Whoever has edited the glossary most recently
An external auditor, in every case
questions.explain: Deciding what a term means to the business is a business judgment — IT can maintain the tool, but shouldn't be deciding what 'Net Revenue' means to Finance.

questions.q: What happens to a term when it reaches the 'deprecated' state, per this lesson?
options: It is immediately and permanently deleted with no trace
It stays visible, clearly marked as deprecated, so historical references still resolve
It is automatically converted back to 'draft'
It is merged into a random other term
questions.explain: This mirrors the metadata lifecycle's 'retire' stage from Lesson 4 — marking an entry retired rather than deleting it preserves historical traceability.

questions.q: Per this lesson, how does the glossary approval workflow relate to the metadata lifecycle from Lesson 4?
options: Draft and in-review correspond to capture; approved-but-reconfirmed corresponds to maintain; deprecated corresponds to retire
They are completely unrelated processes
The approval workflow replaces the need for a metadata lifecycle entirely
Only the 'approved' state has any connection to the metadata lifecycle
questions.explain: The approval workflow is simply the metadata lifecycle's capture and maintain stages made concrete for one specific artifact — the glossary term.
